html:
The military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868, from the city of Edo, modern Tokyo. Its two and a half centuries are called the Edo period, a long peace after a century of civil war.

Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, finishing the work of unification begun by Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi. He became shogun in 1603. The emperor stayed in Kyoto as a figurehead.

How the system worked:

  • About 260 daimyo, regional lords, ran their own domains but had to spend every other year in Edo, leaving their families there as hostages.
  • Society was ranked into samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants, and the sword hunt of 1588 had already taken weapons from commoners.
  • After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 to 1638, Christianity was banned and the country was closed. Of the Europeans, only the Dutch could trade, from the island of Dejima in Nagasaki; Chinese, Korean and Ryukyuan trade went on under tight control.

Peace brought growth. Farmland spread, roads like the Tokaido linked the cities, and Edo grew to more than a million people. Merchants grew rich, and the Dojima Rice Exchange traded rice futures. City culture flourished in kabuki, the haiku of Basho and woodblock prints like The Great Wave.

The end began when Commodore Perry's ships arrived in 1853 and forced Japan to open its ports. The unequal treaties that followed discredited the shogunate. Domains in the southwest rose against it, and in 1868 the Meiji Restoration returned power to the emperor.
sum: The military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868, from the city of Edo, modern Tokyo. Its two and a half centuries are called the Edo period, a long peace after a century of civil war.
